title: import: Reuse Code That Someone Else Already Wrote
excerpt: Load Python's built-in modules with import, choose between import, from-import and aliases, and split your own code into a module.

headings.text: Some Tools Are Not Loaded by Default
When a Module Does Not Exist
Importing Runs the File Only Once

html:
Python can do far more than the handful of functions available the moment you start it. Need square roots, dates or random numbers? Someone has already written that code, tested it and shipped it with Python. You only have to ask for it.

A module is a file of ready-made Python code, and import is the statement that loads it so you can use what is inside. This lesson shows the three ways to import, what happens when a module is missing, and how to turn one of your own files into a module.

Some Tools Are Not Loaded by Default

The function for square roots lives in a module called math. Try to use it without asking for it:

print(sqrt(16))
NameError: name 'sqrt' is not defined

The NameError means Python does not recognise that name. It does not know sqrt, because it has not loaded the math module yet. Add one line to bring it in, and use the module's name followed by a dot to reach what is inside:

import math

print(math.sqrt(16))
print(math.pi)
print(math.factorial(5))
4.0
3.141592653589793
120

The pattern module.name keeps things tidy: reading math.sqrt tells you exactly where sqrt comes from.

Three Ways to Import

You can import the whole module, pick out only the names you need, or give the module a shorter nickname:

import math
from math import sqrt, pi
import statistics as stats

print(math.sqrt(25))
print(sqrt(25))
print(pi)
print(stats.mean([2, 4, 6, 8]))
5.0
5.0
3.141592653589793
5
  • import math loads everything; you write math.sqrt(...).
  • from math import sqrt, pi loads only those names; you write sqrt(...) directly.
  • import statistics as stats loads the module under a shorter name, called an alias.

Which style should you use? For beginners, import module is the clearest, because every use shows where the name comes from. Use from ... import for a few names you use constantly. Avoid from math import *, which dumps every name into your program and makes it hard to tell where anything came from.

When a Module Does Not Exist

If you misspell a module name, or it is not installed, Python tells you clearly:

import not_a_real_module
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'not_a_real_module'

Modules that are not part of Python itself, written by other people, need to be installed first, which means downloading them to your computer. That is a separate step, handled by a tool called pip; a bundle of modules published for others to download is called a package.

Make Your Own Module

Any Python file can be a module, and the module's name is the file's name without .py. Suppose you save this file as greetings.py in your project folder (the f before the quotes lets you put variables inside {}, and the capital letters in GREETING_COUNT signal a value that is not meant to change):

greetings.py

def hello(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

GREETING_COUNT = 2

Save a second file in the same folder and run it with python your_file.py. It imports the first one exactly like a built-in module:

import greetings

print(greetings.hello("Asha"))
print(greetings.GREETING_COUNT)
Hello, Asha!
2

This is how real programs grow: instead of one huge file, you group related functions into modules and import what you need.

Importing Runs the File Only Once

When Python imports a module, it runs the file from top to bottom. But what if two parts of your program both import it? Here is a module that prints a message as soon as it loads:

chatty.py

print("chatty.py is loading")

def ping():
    return "pong"
import chatty
import chatty

print(chatty.ping())
chatty.py is loading
pong

The message appeared only once, even though there are two import lines. Python remembers modules it has already loaded and reuses them, so importing the same module in many places is cheap and safe.

Get the Code

Every example in this lesson, with its output, is in a notebook on GitHub: PythonImportModules.ipynb.

Summary

  • A module is a file of Python code; import loads it so you can use its contents.
  • import math keeps names behind the module, as in math.sqrt(16).
  • from math import sqrt imports specific names, and import statistics as stats creates a short alias.
  • Avoid from module import *; it hides where names come from.
  • A missing or misspelled module raises ModuleNotFoundError.
  • Your own .py file is a module too, and importing a module runs it only once.
